property_summary: For any caller and any sent ETH amount, the reference contract accepts the fallback call (does not revert) iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant changes this rule to require 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference accepts but the mutant reverts (and vice versa).

For every call to C.fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether (so any call with msg.value == 10 ether completes successfully); the mutant requiring 5 ether instead will cause some inputs (e.g. value == 10 ether) that succeed on the reference to revert on the mutant, breaking this rule.

For every caller and sent ETH amount, the reference contract's payable fallback accepts (does not revert) iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts only when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs that make the reference succeed but the mutant revert (or vice versa).

For every caller and amount, calling C's payable fallback succeeds (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that changes the required value to 5 ether will cause some fuzzed msg.value inputs to flip success/failure, so the universal rule (fallback succeeds iff value == 10 ether) is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For every caller and sent ETH amount, calling C's payable fallback succeeds (does not revert) iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant that changes the required value to 5 ether will cause some fuzzed msg.value inputs to flip success/failure (so there exist inputs where reference accepts but mutant reverts).

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so after a successful call pastBlockTime == block.timestamp), while the mutant with inverted comparison can block such calls or fail to update pastBlockTime for inputs where block.timestamp is not less than the prior stored value, causing divergence.

For any caller and any block timestamp/number, when exactly 10 ether is sent to C via its payable fallback the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp after the call (so getter pastBlockTime == block.timestamp), whereas the mutant that requires block.timestamp < pastBlockTime will sometimes revert or not update pastBlockTime, violating this property for some fuzz inputs.

For any caller and any block timestamp/number, when exactly 10 ether is sent to C via its payable fallback, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so c.pastBlockTime() == block.timestamp after the call); the mutant inverts the timestamp check and will sometimes revert or fail to update pastBlockTime, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C's payable fallback, the reference contract always accepts and sets pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so c.pastBlockTime() == block.timestamp after the call); the mutant that inverts the timestamp check can revert or refuse to update pastBlockTime for some prior pastBlockTime/timestamp combinations, breaking this rule.

For any call to C's payable fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so c.pastBlockTime() == block.timestamp after the call); the mutant inverting the timestamp comparison can revert or fail to update pastBlockTime for some prior pastBlockTime/timestamp combinations, breaking this rule.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and with block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract transfers the entire contract balance to msg.sender when block.number % 15 == 0, but the mutant sometimes sends only 1 wei so the rule 'if block.number % 15 == 0 then address(c).balance == 0 after the call' holds for the reference for all admissible inputs and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than the previous call, when block.number % 15 == 0 the reference implementation always transfers the contract's entire balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0) while the mutant may transfer only 1 wei and thus sometimes leaves a nonzero balance; the test asserts address(c).balance == 0 after such a call, which the correct C always satisfies and the mutant violates for some fuzzed block.number/timestamp settings.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than the previous call, if block.number % 15 == 0 then the caller receives exactly address(c).balance (i.e. the contract's balance becomes 0); the mutant that pays only 1 wei will sometimes leave a nonzero balance and thus violate this.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than the previous call, if block.number % 15 == 0 then the reference contract transfers its entire balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0) while the mutant that only transfers 1 wei will leave a nonzero balance for some admissible inputs.

For any caller that sends exactly 10 ether to fallback at a strictly later timestamp than the prior call, if block.number is a multiple of 15 then the caller's balance increases by the entire pre-call contract balance (i.e., the contract's balance becomes 0); the mutant that sends only 1 wei instead breaks this because the caller's balance then increases by far less than the contract's full pre-call balance for some inputs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any sender at any strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract never reverts and when block.number % 15 == 0 it transfers its balance out leaving address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that inserts a revert on that branch can cause the call to revert (breaking the universal successful-call rule) and thus change c's balance outcome for some block numbers.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C at a strictly increasing timestamp, the fallback call always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract; the mutant that inserts a revert when block.number % 15 == 0 causes some such calls to revert, violating this universal-success property.

For any sender that sends exactly 10 ether to C at a strictly increasing timestamp, the fallback call always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract; the mutant that inserts a revert when block.number % 15 == 0 causes some such calls to revert, violating this universal-success property.

For any sender, amount == 10 ether, and strictly increasing timestamp, calling C's fallback always returns (does not revert); the mutant that inserts a revert on block.number % 15 == 0 makes some such calls revert, violating the universal non-revert property.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C at a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference contract's fallback always returns (does not revert) — the mutant that inserts a revert on the branch block.number % 15 == 0 will cause some such calls to revert, violating this universal non-revert property.
